steps.text: Part 2 of 3: Checks, captures, threats: look at the forcing moves first. This part covers Near misses and a mixed test; A real game; Say it back. Each part is short on purpose: finish one, play a game or take a break, and come back.

A **near miss** changes one detail, and the result may flip. Study the original, then ask what the detail did. Details that matter: who can take the checking piece, how many defenders a piece has, whether the king has a flight square. Details that do not: a pawn far from the action. Predict each, then check.
steps.chapter: Near misses and a mixed test

steps.title: One pawn, one square
steps.prompt: The first position is a mate in two. In the second a black pawn stands on b7 instead of a7. In the third a white pawn stands on a3 instead of a2. Predict each, then check.

steps.caption: Now the capture board again, with one change: a black pawn stands on h5, so the bishop on g4 has a second defender. White to move.

line.say: The pawn retakes. This time the queen has nothing to take: pieces were traded evenly.

steps.caption: And a different change: the black a-pawn stands on a6, far from the action. Does the capture still win a piece?

line.say: The same win. The pawn on a6 changed nothing.

steps.text: Kotov's method, as summarised on Wikipedia [S], is to list candidate moves and analyse them in an organised tree. A reviewer of Aagaard's *Excelling at Chess Calculation* says he stresses that big errors often start when a key candidate is never listed [S, reviewer]. [R] Kotov also urged looking at each line once. [I] Checks, captures and threats are the cheapest candidates to list. Now the labels come off. Some positions have a forcing win; some do not, and then saying so is the right answer.

**A very old game**, traditionally credited to Légal and recalled here from memory [R]; the exact record is traditional. The last three White moves are all forcing. First the opening moves, then the moment to list White's forcing moves.

steps.caption: The opening moves. Black's bishop on g4 pins the knight on f3 to the queen on d1.

line.say: The bishop pins the knight to the queen.
Black makes room for the bishop. This move allows a trap, shown next.

claims.statement: The bishop on g4 attacks the knight on f3, with the queen behind it.

steps.caption: White to move. White has two checks (Bxf7+ and Bb5+) and two captures (Nxe5 and Bxf7+). Which works?

claims.statement: Nxe5 is the engine's best move.
Bxf7+ is clearly worse than Nxe5.
Bb5+ is clearly worse than Nxe5.

steps.caption: Black took the queen, which was the mistake: taking the knight was better. White to move. Now the forcing moves finish the game.

line.say: The bishop takes a pawn with check. The king has only one square, e7.
The knight checks from d5 and covers f6, while the knight on e5 and the bishop on f7 cover the other squares: checkmate.

steps.text: Check your answer. Did you say **when** the habit works? Did you say **when it fails**? Did you give an example someone could set up on a board? Did you name **one mistake** (a check that can be taken, a capture that costs more, a threat that is slower)? This is for you to compare with the checklist.

**What to remember.**
- Forcing moves: checks, captures, threats.
- List them first. Then look at every reply.
- A check has few answers: take it, block it, or move the king.
- Forcing is not the same as good.
- Run the opponent's list before you move.
- Nothing forcing works? Say so, and move on.

steps.prompt: Make it concrete. In your next game, on which move will you first stop and list the opponent's checks, captures and threats?

fields.label: I will list them on move number:

steps.text: **Remember.** List checks, captures and threats first, then look at every reply. A check can be taken, blocked or run from. One small detail, such as who can take the checker, can flip the result, while a faraway pawn changes nothing. Forcing is not the same as good, so run the opponent's list too before you move.
